title: Capital Offences
intro: lunes, inglés, marzo — all lowercase in Spanish, all capitalised in English. The one rule that runs backwards from what you'd expect.

options: I have an English class on Monday.
I have an English class on monday.
I have an english class on Monday.
A2.why: Days of the week and languages always take a capital in English.

options: My birthday is in March.
My birthday is in march.
My birthday is in the March.
A2.why: Months take a capital in English, unlike “marzo” in Spanish.

options: She is Spanish.
She is spanish.
She is a Spanish.
A2.why: Nationality adjectives take a capital, with no “a” before them.

options: He speaks English and French.
He speaks english and french.
He speaks English and french.
A2.why: Every language name takes a capital: English, French.

options: My friend and I went to the cinema.
My friend and i went to the cinema.
Me and I went to the cinema.
A2.why: “I” is always a capital, wherever it appears in the sentence.

options: I live in Spain.
I live in spain.
I live in the Spain.
A2.why: Countries take a capital and, like Spain, usually no “the”.

options: Doctor Smith is here.
doctor Smith is here.
Doctor smith is here.
A2.why: A title before a name, and the name itself, both take capitals.

options: We don't have school on Saturday.
We don't have school on saturday.
we don't have school on Saturday.
A2.why: The first word of a sentence takes a capital, and so do days of the week.

options: They are British.
They are british.
They are a British.
A2.why: Nationality adjectives take a capital, with no “a” before them.

options: The sheriff lives in Dallas.
The sheriff lives in dallas.
The Sheriff lives in dallas.
A2.why: City names always take a capital; a job like “sheriff” doesn't.

options: We celebrate Fallas in March.
We celebrate Fallas in march.
We celebrate fallas in march.
A2.why: Months and festivals take capitals in English.

options: My grandmother speaks Valencian.
My grandmother speaks valencian.
my grandmother speaks Valencian.
A2.why: Language names take a capital: Valencian, Spanish, English.

B1.q: Nationalities as nouns — which is correct?
options: Many Spaniards travel abroad in August.
Many spaniards travel abroad in August.
Many Spaniards travel abroad in august.
B1.why: Nationality nouns (Spaniards) and months (August) both take capitals.

options: I've just read The Great Gatsby.
I've just read the great gatsby.
I've just read The great Gatsby.
B1.why: In titles, the main words take capitals; “the” only when it comes first.

B1.q: Days in a list — which is correct?
options: The shop is open on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays.
The shop is open on mondays, wednesdays and fridays.
The shop is open on Mondays, wednesdays and Fridays.
B1.why: Every day of the week takes a capital, even in a list.

options: He studies Buddhism at university.
He studies buddhism at university.
He studies Buddhism at University.
B1.why: Religions take a capital; “university” as a general word doesn't.

options: She grew up in the south of Spain.
She grew up in the south of spain.
She grew up in the South of spain.
B1.why: “The south of Spain” is just a direction, so lowercase; Spain always takes a capital.

options: I bought it at Zara.
I bought it at zara.
I bought it at the Zara.
B1.why: Brand names take a capital, and a shop name like Zara needs no “the”.

options: The meeting is on 3 April.
The meeting is on 3 april.
The meeting is on the 3rd of april.
B1.why: Months keep their capital in dates too: 3 April.

options: We studied the Renaissance last year.
We studied the renaissance last year.
We studied The renaissance last year.
B1.why: Named historical periods take a capital: the Renaissance.

B1.q: Nationalities as adjectives — which is correct?
options: I love Italian food.
I love italian food.
I love Italian Food.
B1.why: Nationality adjectives take a capital; ordinary nouns like “food” don't.

options: Cowboys were part of the Wild West.
Cowboys were part of the wild west.
Cowboys were part of the Wild west.
B1.why: “The Wild West” is a name, so both words take capitals.

options: The chemist's is on Colón Street.
The chemist's is on colón street.
The chemist's is on Colón street.
B1.why: A street name is a proper name: every word takes a capital.

options: We always go home for Easter.
We always go home for easter.
We always go Home for Easter.
B1.why: Festivals like Easter take a capital; ordinary nouns like “home” don't.

options: She works for the United Nations.
She works for the united nations.
She works for the United nations.
B2.why: Each main word in an institution's name takes a capital.

B2.q: Directions as regions — which is correct?
options: Relations between Russia and the West have worsened.
Relations between Russia and the west have worsened.
relations between Russia and the West have worsened.
B2.why: “The West” as a political bloc is usually capitalised.

B2.q: Literal compass directions — which is correct?
options: Turn west at the next junction.
Turn West at the next junction.
turn west at the next junction.
B2.why: As a simple direction on the road, “west” is lowercase.

options: The exhibition celebrates Maori culture.
The exhibition celebrates maori culture.
The exhibition celebrates Maori Culture.
B2.why: Names of peoples take a capital; “culture” itself doesn't.

B2.q: Job titles as generic nouns — which is correct?
options: My father is a doctor.
My father is a Doctor.
my father is a doctor.
B2.why: A job used as a general noun stays lowercase: a doctor.

B2.q: Job titles before a name — which is correct?
options: I spoke to Professor García.
I spoke to professor García.
I spoke to Professor garcía.
B2.why: A title directly before a name takes a capital: Professor García.

options: I'm studying history and Spanish.
I'm studying History and Spanish.
I'm studying history and spanish.
B2.why: School subjects are lowercase, except languages, which always take capitals.

options: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun.
mars is the fourth planet from the sun.
Mars is the fourth Planet from the sun.
B2.why: Planets take a capital; in astronomy the Sun usually does too, though it's optional. “Planet” itself doesn't.

options: We don't work on Christmas Day.
We don't work on christmas day.
we don't work on Christmas day.
B2.why: Public holidays take a capital on each main word: Christmas Day.

B2.q: Job titles before a name — which is correct?
options: Everyone in town feared Marshal Dillon.
Everyone in town feared marshal Dillon.
Everyone in town feared Marshal dillon.
B2.why: A title directly before a name takes a capital, like the name itself.

B2.q: Job titles as generic nouns — which is correct?
options: John Snow worked as a surgeon in London.
John Snow worked as a Surgeon in London.
John Snow worked as a surgeon in london.
B2.why: A job used as a general noun stays lowercase; London always takes a capital.

options: We visited the Silk Exchange in Valencia.
We visited the silk exchange in Valencia.
We visited the Silk exchange in Valencia.
B2.why: A building's official name takes a capital on each main word.

C1.q: Words from names — which is correct?
options: The Victorians built many of Britain's railway stations.
The victorians built many of Britain's railway stations.
The Victorians Built Many Of Britain's Railway Stations.
C1.why: Words formed from a name, like Victorian (from Queen Victoria), keep the capital.

options: The bill was debated in the House of Commons.
The bill was debated in the house of commons.
The bill was debated in the House of commons.
C1.why: The House of Commons is the name of one specific body, so each main word takes a capital.

options: The Industrial Revolution changed everything.
The industrial revolution changed everything.
The Industrial revolution changed everything.
C1.why: Named historical events take a capital on each main word.

options: The Bible has been translated into many languages.
The bible has been translated into many languages.
the Bible has been translated into many languages.
C1.why: The Bible is the title of a sacred text, so it takes a capital.

options: She wrote a thesis on Marxism.
She wrote a thesis on marxism.
she wrote a thesis on Marxism.
C1.why: Movements named after a person (Marx) keep the capital.

options: He's a Gemini.
He's a gemini.
he's a Gemini.
C1.why: Star signs are names, so they take a capital.

C1.q: Titles before a name — which is correct?
options: The speech was given by King Charles III.
The speech was given by king Charles III.
The speech was given by King charles III.
C1.why: A title directly before a name is part of the name, so it takes a capital: King Charles.

options: Tensions in the Middle East remain high.
Tensions in the middle east remain high.
Tensions in the Middle east remain high.
C1.why: The Middle East is the name of a region: capitals on both words.

C1.q: Brand names with an inner capital — which is correct?
options: She sent the file by WhatsApp.
She sent the file by whatsapp.
She sent the file by Whatsapp.
C1.why: Brand names keep their capitals exactly as the company writes them: WhatsApp.

options: The Black Death reached Valencia in 1348.
The black death reached Valencia in 1348.
The Black death reached Valencia in 1348.
C1.why: Named historical events take a capital on each main word.

options: We moved to Valencia in the spring of 1975.
We moved to Valencia in the Spring of 1975.
We moved to valencia in the spring of 1975.
C1.why: Seasons stay lowercase in English, unlike days and months.

options: The Spanish Civil War began in 1936.
The Spanish civil war began in 1936.
The spanish Civil War began in 1936.
C1.why: A named war takes capitals, and so does the nationality: Spanish.
